content.content:
1	"""Task assignment, dynamic map edits and collision-aware tick execution.
2	
3	Obstacles may be closed and reopened between ticks through
4	:meth:`FleetSimulator.modify_obstacles`. Every accepted edit is appended to a
5	deterministic change history and mirrored into the replay as a ``map_change``
6	event stamped with the tick at which it took effect. Tick frames themselves are
7	never rewritten, so historical frames keep the positions and completion
8	information recorded at the time.
9	
10	Automatic yielding
11	------------------
12	When a robot's next waypoint is occupied by another robot, ``step()`` tries to
13	keep traffic flowing instead of waiting forever: a parked blocker (one with no
14	bound task *and* no remaining route) is asked to move onto a free side cell
15	that lies on no robot's planned route, and a busy robot facing a blocker that
16	cannot drive on may itself sidestep onto a free adjacent cell and replan its
17	(still shortest) route from there. A taskless robot that still carries a
18	remaining route is not parked: it drives that route cell by cell exactly like
19	a task-bound robot, is never pushed onto a side cell for someone else, and if
20	its own next cell is blocked it simply keeps its place and its unconsumed
21	waypoints -- an open side cell changes nothing. Only once such a route is
22	exhausted does the robot become a parked robot and yield by the side-cell
23	rule. Task assignment follows the same line: only a robot with no bound task
24	*and* no remaining route can receive a waiting task, so a taskless robot
25	still driving its preset route never has that route overwritten by a new
26	assignment -- being blocked by traffic along the way does not count as having
27	finished the route, and once the route runs out the robot joins the selection
28	at the next assignment pass, planned from wherever it stands then. A retreat that
29	only leads back to the same immovable blocker is never taken though: if the
30	replanned route immediately returns through the vacated cell, still passes the
31	blocker's cell and the blocker cannot use the opening to leave (a dead end or
32	corridor end with traffic parked beyond it), the robot simply waits -- extra
33	empty cells stretching out behind it change nothing. Nor does the blocker's
34	own side step automatically count as leaving: when that step only moves the
35	blocker onto a side cell whose replanned route returns it onto the corridor
36	to face the very same unyielding jam further ahead, the opening is no opening
37	and the retreat behind it is rejected as well. Yield moves count as
38	mileage, waiting does not. The task keeps its original robot, pickup and
39	completion rules are unchanged, and a robot paused by map unreachability never
40	takes part in yielding. If no safe side cell exists the robots simply wait:
41	time advances, nothing collides and nothing completes early. Waiting caused
42	purely by other robots is tracked per robot (consecutive ticks and the
43	blocking robot) and reported by :meth:`FleetSimulator.status` and
44	:meth:`FleetSimulator.metrics` as ``traffic_waits``, distinct from the
45	map-unreachability ``paused_tasks``. The record is judged against the
46	end-of-tick layout, not the moment the robot gave way: when a robot that was
47	asked to wait sees its next cell free at tick end (the blocker drove on or
48	made room later in the same tick), no wait is reported for that tick at all,
49	and ``blocked_by`` names whichever robot actually occupies the cell once the
50	tick settles. The counter clears the moment the robot moves again or the
51	blockage ends; an uninterrupted wait whose blocking robot merely changes
52	identity keeps accumulating with the new blocker, whereas a wait that was
53	interrupted and later recurs starts again at one. An accepted map edit
54	reconciles the records immediately: a robot paused by the new map or no
55	longer facing its recorded blocker on the replanned route loses its entry, an
56	entry still facing the same blocker keeps its count, and no edit ever creates
57	or increments one.
58	
59	Initial identifiers
60	-------------------
61	Identity is per batch and per kind: each robot id may name at most one robot
62	in the robot list and each task id at most one task in the task list, while
63	the two lists have independent namespaces -- a robot and a task may share one
64	string, a task's owner reference is not a second robot record, and any number
65	of completed tasks may keep the same historical robot, even one absent from
66	the fleet. The identifier alone decides: identical objects passed twice, two
67	robots that differ only in position, idle state, preset route or current task,
68	and two tasks that differ in pickup/dropoff, owner or completion (one already
69	finished beside one still waiting) are all rejected. Nothing keeps one copy,
70	merges the records or renames them -- the whole request raises
71	:class:`ValueError` saying whether the clash is in the robots or the tasks and
72	quoting the duplicated id. The check is read-only and runs before any
73	normalization commits, so even a duplicate at the end of either list leaves
74	every earlier object -- positions, list-shaped routes and points, bindings,
75	mileage and flags -- exactly as supplied; tasks distinct in id but equal in
76	pickup/dropoff stay distinct records and both take part in assignment and
77	completion statistics. Checkpoint files keep their own pre-existing duplicate
78	id rejection unchanged.
79	
80	Initial task ownership
81	----------------------
82	A fleet can be created mid-work: a robot may already name its current task
83	with a remaining route, and a task may already be assigned or even loaded.
84	Construction validates these bindings up front instead of discovering them
85	while stepping. Every robot that names a task must name one that exists, is
86	still unfinished and is assigned back to that robot; every unfinished task
87	that names an owner must name an existing robot whose current task it is, and
88	a task with the goods collected may never lack that owner. One robot is
89	therefore never claimed by two unfinished tasks, and a robot may never be
90	bound to a completed task. A finished task is a fixed historical record and
91	must carry both the picked-up mark and the historical robot that finished it:
92	``assigned_robot`` of ``None`` means the record is missing, not an anonymous
93	completion, and the mark is never presumed -- not even when the task's pickup
94	point and dropoff are the same cell. Finished tasks only retain *historical*
95	ownership: their recorded robot need not be idle or name them back, may
96	already work a new task, may have finished several tasks, and may even be
97	absent from the fleet, so history never occupies a robot or enters new task
98	assignment. Unassigned, not-yet-collected tasks simply wait -- including ones
99	no robot can currently reach -- and are not an ownership error. Conflicts
100	raise :class:`ValueError` naming the robot or task and the contradiction
101	involved; nothing is rebound, unassigned or dropped, and the caller's objects
102	are left untouched. The very same ownership and completed-history rules
103	govern checkpoint loading, so a completion record one entry point accepts
104	can never be a record the other cannot reload.
105	
106	Every task's pickup point and dropoff is validated with the very same strict
107	coordinate rule as robot positions (:func:`_as_cell`): each must be a list or
108	tuple holding exactly two plain integers, and the two spellings may be mixed
109	freely within one task and across one batch. A boolean is never an integer
110	here -- not even ``True`` for a 1-coordinate -- and a float is refused even
111	when it equals an integer value such as ``1.0``; strings, nulls, scalars,
112	missing components, extra components and anything that is not a coordinate
113	pair all raise :class:`ValueError` naming the task id and whether its pickup
114	or its dropoff is at fault -- nothing is rounded, padded or coerced into a
115	pair, so a fleet can never accept a task that its own checkpoint loading
116	would later reject. An accepted point is normalized to a fresh integer tuple
117	(``[1, 0]`` and ``(1, 0)`` therefore name one cell: a robot can neither miss
118	a pickup nor fail a delivery merely because the containers differ), and the
119	copy means a caller that keeps mutating its original coordinate lists after
120	construction can never change the created fleet. The rule covers every task
121	regardless of state -- waiting for assignment, already assigned and heading
122	to pickup, carrying the goods, and finished historical records alike. Like
123	position normalization, the points commit nothing until the whole batch
124	(positions, ownership, routes and all task points) has passed: a failure on a
125	later task point, robot route or binding leaves every earlier task holding
126	its original pickup/dropoff containers and every flag, binding, route and
127	mileage exactly as passed in. Coordinate validity and current reachability
128	are deliberately separate judgements: a well-formed task no robot can
129	currently reach simply keeps waiting, and a loaded task whose pickup cell has
130	since been closed keeps the goods and its owner -- neither is a coordinate
131	error, and selection order, planning, obstacle handling and completion
132	history behave exactly as before. Checkpoints keep their integer coordinate
133	arrays and strict loading rules unchanged -- no format bump and no
134	relaxation.
135	
136	Every robot's starting position is validated with the very same strict
137	coordinate rule its route waypoints use (:func:`_as_cell`): it must be a list
138	or tuple holding exactly two plain integers, and the two spellings may be
139	mixed freely within one batch. A boolean is never an integer here, and floats,
140	strings, missing or extra components and anything that is not a coordinate
141	pair all raise :class:`ValueError` naming the robot and its offending starting
142	position -- nothing is rounded, coerced or padded into a pair. An accepted
143	position is normalized to a fresh integer tuple (``[0, 0]`` and ``(0, 0)``
144	therefore create identical fleets that move and receive tasks identically),
145	and the copy means a caller that keeps mutating its original list after
146	construction can never change the created fleet. Positions must lie inside
147	the map and outside every obstacle, and no two robots may start on the same
148	cell: the comparison is made on the normalized coordinate values, so a list
149	and a tuple naming one cell still collide, and the error names both robots.
150	This covers every robot regardless of task state -- unbound, task-executing
151	and preset-route robots alike -- so a batch can never succeed by ignoring one
152	robot. Like the route check, position normalization commits nothing until the
153	entire batch (positions, ownership and routes) has passed: a failure on a
154	later robot's route or task binding leaves every earlier robot's original
155	position object, remaining route and task binding exactly as passed in.
156	
157	Every robot's remaining route is also validated as a walk on the given map,
158	whether or not the robot is bound to a task, and direct construction and
159	checkpoint recovery run the *same* :func:`_validate_route_walk` check, so the
160	walking rule is maintained in exactly one place. The route omits the robot's
161	current cell, so a non-empty route must begin with an up/down/left/right
162	neighbour of that cell and every later waypoint must be one orthogonal step
163	from the previous one; each waypoint must be in bounds and free of obstacles.
164	Diagonal steps, multi-cell jumps, two identical consecutive waypoints and a
165	first waypoint equal to the current position are all rejected, and waypoints
166	must be two plain integers (never booleans) in a list or tuple, with wrong
167	lengths or element types raising :class:`ValueError` rather than leaking
168	unpacking or hashing errors. Empty routes stay legal; a route need not be
169	shortest and may revisit cells. A route crossing another robot's current cell,
170	or several robots planning through the same cell, is not an error -- those
171	traffic conflicts are settled during execution. The direct interface keeps
172	its existing acceptance of a bound route's pickup/dropoff ordering and end
173	point; checkpoint loading additionally keeps its own stricter route checks
174	(including the task completion rules), its format and the map-paused
175	behaviour, under which a paused robot resumes with an empty route.
176	
177	Direct construction always judges every waypoint against the map handed to
178	it, so a route crossing an initial obstacle is rejected no matter the robot's
179	task state. Checkpoint recovery owns exactly one relaxation, and only for a
180	version 2 document: a robot with no bound task keeps its remaining preset
181	waypoints when a later map edit closes the cell ahead -- it simply waits
182	before it -- so such a waypoint may be blocked on the saved map provided it
183	was traversable on the base map, some recorded change net-closes it and it is
184	still closed at save time. The set of cells this can possibly cover is
185	derived from the already validated ``base_grid`` plus ``map_changes``, never
186	from the route itself: a base-map obstacle and any blocked cell the history
187	cannot explain stay rejected, version 1 files (which carry no history) keep
188	the old rule, and a task-bound robot never qualifies. Out-of-bounds,
189	malformed and non-adjacent waypoints are rejected for every robot either
190	way. After reopening, the restored robot keeps driving the same cells in the
191	same order: waiting neither consumes a waypoint nor adds mileage, and the
192	route is never replanned into a shortcut.
193	
194	Checkpoint file format
195	----------------------
196	``save_checkpoint`` writes versioned, UTF-8 encoded JSON. The current format
197	version is ``2``; version ``1`` files remain readable.
198	
199	``version``
200	    Integer format version (``1`` or ``2``).
201	``grid``
202	    ``{"width": int, "height": int, "obstacles": [[x, y], ...]}`` describing
203	    the map dimensions and every currently blocked cell.
204	``tick``
205	    Non-negative integer: the number of ticks already executed. Saving and
206	    loading never advance this value.
207	``robots``
208	    List of robot states, each
209	    ``{"robot_id": str, "position": [x, y], "route": [[x, y], ...],
210	    "task_id": str | null, "distance_travelled": int}``. ``route`` holds the
211	    remaining waypoints after ``position`` (empty for a paused robot). For a
212	    taskless robot the route may head into a cell the change history has
213	    closed and the saved grid still shows blocked: the robot is simply waiting
214	    there with its preset waypoints intact, and loading restores that wait.
215	``tasks``
216	    List of task states, each
217	    ``{"task_id": str, "pickup": [x, y], "dropoff": [x, y],
218	    "assigned_robot": str | null, "picked_up": bool, "completed": bool}``.
219	    Completed tasks keep their historical ``assigned_robot``: a task saved as
220	    completed must also be marked picked up and name the robot that finished
221	    it (never null), and loading rejects a record missing either half with the
222	    same rule direct fleet construction enforces.
223	``replay``
224	    Ordered event list. Tick events are numbered consecutively from ``1``
225	    through ``tick`` and have the shape
226	    ``{"type": "tick", "tick": int, "moved": [robot_id, ...],
227	    "robots": {robot_id: [x, y], ...}, "completed": [task_id, ...]}``.
228	    ``completed`` is the cumulative set of tasks finished by the end of that
229	    tick: entries must name checkpoint tasks without repeats within one frame,
230	    a recorded completion must survive every later frame, and the final
231	    frame's set must equal the tasks saved with ``completed: true``.
232	    Map-change events sit between ticks (or after the last tick) and look like
233	    ``{"type": "map_change", "tick": int, "sequence": int,
234	    "added": [[x, y], ...], "removed": [[x, y], ...]}``. When ``tick`` is
235	    non-zero the final tick event's robot positions must match the current
236	    robot positions.
237	``map_changes`` (version 2 only)
238	    List mirroring the replay map-change events in the same order:
239	    ``{"tick": int, "sequence": int, "added": [...], "removed": [...]}``.
240	``base_grid`` (version 2 only)
241	    ``{"width", "height", "obstacles"}`` describing the map before any runtime
242	    edit. Replaying ``map_changes`` against it must reproduce the saved current
243	    ``grid``.
244	``traffic_waits`` (optional)
245	    List of ``{"robot_id": str, "blocked_by": [str, ...], "ticks": int}``
246	    entries recording how many consecutive ticks each robot has been held up
247	    purely by other robots. Absent in older files, which load with every
248	    wait counter at zero. Each entry must agree with the saved layout: the
249	    robot needs a remaining route and ``blocked_by`` must name exactly the
250	    robot occupying its next route cell -- a next cell nobody occupies, a
251	    listed blocker parked elsewhere, or extra names beside the real blocker
252	    all reject the document.
253	
254	Version 1 documents store tick frames without a ``type`` field and have no
255	``map_changes`` or ``base_grid`` key; they load with their grid taken as the
256	baseline, as if no map edit ever happened.
257	
258	The ordinary-tick-frame rules both versions share -- the replay container is
259	a list, every frame is an object, and tick frames are numbered consecutively
260	from 1 with a well-formed payload -- are owned by the single shared
261	:meth:`FleetSimulator._iter_replay_events` scan, so they are maintained in
262	exactly one place. Each version keeps its own handling on top: version 1
263	rejects non-tick frames and fills in the missing ``type`` on a copy, while
264	version 2 dispatches event types and enforces its map-change ordering.
265	
266	Both map definitions are validated by the single shared
267	:meth:`FleetSimulator._load_map_definition` rule -- positive integer
268	dimensions, an obstacle list of integer ``[x, y]`` pairs inside the map --
269	with wording that names the map at fault, so a format or value rule is
270	maintained in exactly one place while each map keeps its own contents. The
271	cross-definition constraints (matching dimensions and a history that replays
272	``base_grid`` onto ``grid``) are checked separately and remain distinct
273	rejection reasons from a malformed definition.
274	
275	Loading performs strict validation: malformed JSON, missing or wrongly typed
276	fields, unsupported versions, duplicate or inconsistent entities, out of
277	bounds/obstructed positions and routes, non-adjacent route steps, ownership
278	mismatches, routes that cannot finish the robot's bound task, traffic waits
279	that contradict the saved robot positions and remaining routes, broken replay
280	or map-change history, a completion history that contradicts the saved task
281	states, and a history that does not reproduce the saved grid all raise
282	:class:`ValueError`.
283	
284	The single route-walk exception recovery allows is a preset-route robot that
285	is waiting out a dynamic closure. In a version 2 file a robot without a bound
286	task may keep waypoints that are blocked on the saved grid when the base map
287	had the cell open and the recorded change history explains its current,
288	still-effective closure (a cell closed and reopened before the save is open
289	again and therefore never covered). Such a robot was produced by normal
290	running -- closing a cell never strips a taskless robot of its remaining
291	route, the robot just waits before the cell -- so recovery restores it as is
292	and it drives on, same cells, same order, once the cell reopens. The
293	exemption cannot reach anything else: direct fleet construction has no
294	history and rejects routes through initial obstacles, a blocked waypoint the
295	history cannot account for (including every blocked waypoint in a version 1
296	document) is still rejected, and robots bound to a task never qualify --
297	their routes are replanned or their tasks paused at edit time and load under
298	the unchanged task rules. A robot standing on an obstacle and an out-of-map,
299	malformed or non-adjacent waypoint are rejected regardless of task state.
300	
301	A task-bound route is judged against the task's pickup state, not just for
302	walkability. For every assigned, unfinished task that is not paused by map
303	unreachability, a non-empty remaining route must end at the dropoff, and when
304	the goods are not yet collected and the robot is not already standing on the
305	pickup cell, the route must still pass through that pickup cell -- passing the
306	dropoff early changes nothing as long as the route later collects and returns,
307	and avoidance detours need not match a replanned shortest route. An empty
308	route is accepted only when a loaded robot already stands at the dropoff, or
309	when position, pickup and dropoff all coincide; paused tasks keep their
310	empty-route exemption, and unassigned or completed tasks are not checked.
311	
312	The recorded movement history is checked for physical plausibility, not just
313	for a matching final frame. In every tick frame each robot must stand on a
314	cell that is in bounds and traversable on the map of that moment, no two
315	robots may end a tick on the same cell, and from the second frame on a robot
316	may only have waited or stepped one orthogonal cell (two robots cannot swap
317	cells within one tick; following a robot into the cell it just vacated is
318	fine). A frame's ``moved`` list must reference current fleet robots without
319	duplicates and, whenever a previous frame exists, must name exactly the
320	robots whose positions changed, in any order. Version 2 map changes are
321	applied in their recorded order after the tick they are stamped on, so a
322	robot may be recorded in a cell that is closed later, may not appear in a
323	cell before it opens, and no change may add an obstacle onto a cell a tick
324	frame shows occupied -- not even when a later change of the same tick removes
325	it. Filesystem and permission failures propagate as :class:`OSError`.

345	def _is_int(value: object) -> bool:
346	    """JSON booleans are ints in Python; checkpoints treat them as wrong."""
347	    return isinstance(value, int) and not isinstance(value, bool)

350	def _coordinate_pair(value: object, description: str, *, strict_list: bool) -> Position:
351	    """Validate *value* as a pair of two plain integers.
352	
353	    Booleans are rejected even though they are Python ints, and wrong lengths
354	    or element types raise :class:`ValueError` instead of leaking unpacking or
355	    hashing errors. This is the one coordinate-shape rule shared by every
356	    caller; the two entry points only differ in the outer container spellings
357	    they accept:
358	
359	    * strict JSON lists only (*strict_list* true, checkpoints, whose document
360	      shape is fixed and must not be relaxed because validation is shared);
361	    * lists or tuples alike (*strict_list* false, the direct Python interface,
362	      where the two spellings may be mixed freely).
363	    """
364	    if strict_list:
365	        # Checkpoints keep their single, fixed message for every shape problem
366	        # -- wrong type, wrong length or a non-integer (including a boolean) --
367	        # because the JSON document shape is fixed and shared validation must
368	        # not change what a malformed checkpoint reports.
369	        if (
370	            not isinstance(value, list)
371	            or len(value) != 2
372	            or not all(_is_int(coord) for coord in value)
373	        ):
374	            raise ValueError(f"{description} must be a [x, y] integer pair")
375	    else:
376	        if isinstance(value, (str, bytes)) or not isinstance(value, (tuple, list)):
377	            raise ValueError(f"{description} must be a [x, y] integer pair")
378	        if len(value) != 2:
379	            raise ValueError(f"{description} must be a [x, y] integer pair")
380	        if not all(_is_int(coord) for coord in value):
381	            raise ValueError(
382	                f"{description} coordinates must be integers, not booleans or other types"
383	            )
384	    return value[0], value[1]
385

387	def _as_cell(value: object, description: str) -> Position:
388	    """Validate a user supplied coordinate as a two-integer list or tuple."""
389	    return _coordinate_pair(value, description, strict_list=False)

392	def _as_pair(value: object, description: str) -> tuple[int, int]:
393	    """Validate a checkpoint coordinate as a two-integer JSON list."""
394	    return _coordinate_pair(value, description, strict_list=True)

397	def _task_route_waypoints(origin: Position, task: Task) -> list[Position]:
398	    """Required remaining visit points after *origin* for *task*.
399	
400	    The same pickup/delivery rule is used by first-time assignment, rerouting
401	    after map changes (and the recovery/sidestep planning that shares it) and
402	    checkpoint validation, so the requirement lives in exactly one place:
403	
404	    * Goods not yet collected: the route must still reach the pickup and then
405	      the dropoff. Standing exactly on the pickup makes the pickup leg empty --
406	      the leg contributes no waypoint -- but planning never collects or
407	      completes anything by itself.
408	    * Goods already collected: the robot routes straight to the dropoff, even
409	      when the old pickup cell was closed afterwards; it is never sent back.
410	
411	    When *origin*, pickup and dropoff coincide the list is empty, which
412	    describes a feasible zero-step route and must not be confused with an
413	    unreachable one.
414	    """
415	    waypoints: list[Position] = []
416	    if not task.picked_up and origin != task.pickup:
417	        waypoints.append(task.pickup)
418	    last = waypoints[-1] if waypoints else origin
419	    if task.dropoff != last:
420	        waypoints.append(task.dropoff)
421	    return waypoints

424	def _plan_task_route(
425	    grid: GridMap, origin: Position, task: Task
426	) -> list[Position] | None:
427	    """Shortest feasible route through the task's required waypoints.
428	
429	    The returned list holds the cells after *origin* only, concatenating the
430	    deterministic shortest legs between consecutive required points. It is
431	    ``None`` when any required point cannot be reached, and an empty list for a
432	    feasible route with zero steps (origin already at the only destination).
433	    """
434	    route: list[Position] = []
435	    current = origin
436	    for waypoint in _task_route_waypoints(origin, task):
437	        try:
438	            leg = shortest_path(grid, current, waypoint)
439	        except ValueError:
440	            return None
441	        route.extend(leg)
442	        current = waypoint
443	    return route

446	def _validate_route_walk(
447	    grid: GridMap,
448	    origin: Position,
449	    route: Sequence[object],
450	    *,
451	    robot_id: str,
452	    checkpoint: bool,
453	    blocked_cells: frozenset[Position] | None = None,
454	) -> list[Position]:
455	    """Validate one robot's remaining route as a cell-by-cell map walk.
456	
457	    This is the single place that owns the walking rule shared by direct
458	    fleet construction and checkpoint recovery, so the same legality check is
459	    never edited twice. A route holds the cells still ahead of *origin*:
460	
461	    * every waypoint must parse as two plain integers (booleans are rejected),
462	      and lie inside the map -- a cell in *blocked_cells* is the one kind of
463	      currently obstructed waypoint a version 2 checkpoint recovery may carry
464	      (see below), everything else off the traversable map is rejected;
465	    * the first waypoint must be an up/down/left/right neighbour of *origin*,
466	      so a first waypoint equal to the current cell is rejected;
467	    * every later waypoint must be exactly one orthogonal step from the
468	      previous one -- diagonal moves, multi-cell jumps and two identical
469	      consecutive waypoints are all rejected.
470	
471	    Detours and revisits (including *origin*) are legal, and a route crossing
472	    another robot's cell is never a walk error: traffic is settled while
473	    stepping, not here. The walkability rule deliberately says nothing about
474	    the bound task's pickup/dropoff requirements; checkpoint loading keeps
475	    that separate, stricter business check. The result is a fresh mutable list
476	    of tuple cells, so validating never aliases or mutates the caller's
477	    container and a rejected input leaves every earlier object untouched.
478	
479	    *blocked_cells* is honoured only for checkpoint recovery and names the
480	    cells the recorded map-change history explains: cells open on the base map
481	    that an accepted edit has since closed and that are still closed at save
482	    time. A taskless robot's preset route may legitimately end on such a cell
483	    -- the robot keeps its unconsumed waypoints and simply waits before it --
484	    so those waypoints walk as well as the open cells do. The exemption is
485	    deliberately narrow: only checkpoint loading ever supplies the set (direct
486	    construction leaves it ``None``), only a robot without a bound task may
487	    use it (the caller never passes the set for a task route), and the cells
488	    must be inside the map -- an out-of-bounds waypoint is rejected regardless.
489	    A blocked cell in the base map that no edit explains is never part of the
490	    set, so a route crossing an initial or unexplained obstacle stays illegal.
491	
492	    The two entries keep their existing format and wording differences via
493	    *checkpoint*: direct construction (false) accepts a list or tuple route of
494	    list-or-tuple cells and reports ``route waypoint N`` with a dedicated
495	    message for a first waypoint on the current cell and for repeated
496	    consecutive waypoints; checkpoint loading (true) keeps the strict JSON
497	    list-of-lists format (``_as_pair``), says ``route entry`` and folds both
498	    equal-cell cases into its existing non-adjacency message. The checks
499	    performed are identical either way.
500	    """
501	    allowed_blocked = frozenset() if blocked_cells is None else blocked_cells
502	    waypoints: list[Position] = []
503	    previous = origin
504	    for index, cell in enumerate(route):
505	        if checkpoint:
506	            waypoint = _as_pair(
507	                cell, f"robot {robot_id!r} route entry {index}"
508	            )
509	        else:
510	            waypoint = _as_cell(
511	                cell, f"robot {robot_id!r} route waypoint {index}"
512	            )
513	        if not grid.contains(waypoint) or (
514	            waypoint in grid.obstacles and waypoint not in allowed_blocked
515	        ):
516	            if checkpoint:
517	                raise ValueError(
518	                    f"robot {robot_id!r} route entry {list(waypoint)} is "
519	                    "outside the map or inside an obstacle"
520	                )
521	            raise ValueError(
522	                f"robot {robot_id!r} route waypoint {index} "
523	                f"{list(waypoint)} is outside the map or inside an obstacle"
524	            )
525	        if waypoint == previous:
526	            if checkpoint:
527	                # The checkpoint wording treats an equal cell like any other
528	                # non-adjacent step, naming both cells of the offending move.
529	                raise ValueError(
530	                    f"robot {robot_id!r} route moves non-adjacently from "
531	                    f"{list(previous)} to {list(waypoint)}"
532	                )
533	            if index == 0:
534	                raise ValueError(
535	                    f"robot {robot_id!r} route waypoint 0 {list(waypoint)} "
536	                    "is the robot's current cell; the remaining route must "
537	                    "start with the next cell"
538	                )
539	            raise ValueError(
540	                f"robot {robot_id!r} route repeats cell {list(waypoint)} at "
541	                f"consecutive waypoints {index - 1} and {index}"
542	            )
543	        if (
544	            abs(waypoint[0] - previous[0])
545	            + abs(waypoint[1] - previous[1])
546	            != 1
547	        ):
548	            if checkpoint:
549	                raise ValueError(
550	                    f"robot {robot_id!r} route moves non-adjacently from "
551	                    f"{list(previous)} to {list(waypoint)}"
552	                )
553	            if index == 0:
554	                segment = (
555	                    f"from its current position {list(previous)} to route "
556	                    f"waypoint 0 {list(waypoint)}"
557	                )
558	            else:
559	                segment = (
560	                    f"from route waypoint {index - 1} {list(previous)} to "
561	                    f"waypoint {index} {list(waypoint)}"
562	                )
563	            raise ValueError(
564	                f"robot {robot_id!r} route moves non-adjacently {segment}: "
565	                "every step must move one orthogonal cell"
566	            )
567	        waypoints.append(waypoint)
568	        previous = waypoint
569	    return waypoints

572	class FleetSimulator:
573	    def __init__(
574	        self,
575	        grid: GridMap,
576	        robots: list[Robot],
577	        tasks: list[Task],
578	        *,
579	        _routes_prevalidated: bool = False,
580	    ) -> None:
581	        self.grid = grid
582	        # The map as built before any runtime edit; map-change history is
583	        # replayed against this baseline.
584	        self.base_grid = grid
585	        # Identity uniqueness is the first batch check: the same robot id may
586	        # name at most one robot in the request and the same task id at most
587	        # one task. It is read-only and rejects the whole batch before any
588	        # normalization can commit, so a clash leaves every caller object
589	        # exactly as supplied. See :meth:`_require_unique_ids`.
590	        self._require_unique_ids(robots, tasks)
591	        # Starting positions share the route coordinates' strict rule: only a
592	        # list or tuple of two plain integers is accepted (booleans, floats and
593	        # strings never act as coordinates), and every accepted position is
594	        # normalized to a fresh integer tuple before any state is committed.
595	        # Task pickup/dropoff points follow the very same rule. This mirrors
596	        # :meth:`_normalize_initial_routes`: all robots and tasks stay exactly
597	        # as the caller passed them until the whole batch -- positions, task
598	        # points, overlaps, ownership and routes -- has passed.
599	        normalized_positions = self._normalize_start_positions(grid, robots)
600	        normalized_task_points = self._normalize_task_coordinates(tasks)
601	        self.robots = {robot.robot_id: robot for robot in robots}
602	        self.tasks = {task.task_id: task for task in tasks}
603	        self.tick = 0
604	        self.replay: list[dict[str, object]] = []
605	        self.map_changes: list[dict[str, object]] = []
606	        self._map_sequence = 0
607	        self.paused_tasks: set[str] = set()
608	        # Consecutive per-robot waits caused purely by other robots:
609	        # robot_id -> {"blocked_by": [robot_id, ...], "ticks": int}.
610	        self._traffic_waits: dict[str, dict[str, object]] = {}
611	        self._validate_task_ownership(robots, tasks)
612	        if _routes_prevalidated:
613	            # Checkpoint recovery has already run the shared
614	            # :func:`_validate_route_walk` itself -- including its one narrow
615	            # checkpoint exemption for a taskless preset route waiting before
616	            # a history-explained closed cell -- so its already-normalized
617	            # routes must not be re-checked here against the saved grid, where
618	            # those legitimate waypoints look obstructed. Its robots are built
619	            # fresh during loading with validated integer-tuple positions too,
620	            # so nothing needs committing here. Every other constructor check
621	            # above still ran.
622	            return
623	        # Accepted positions, routes and task points share one internal shape
624	        # regardless of how the caller spelled them: an integer tuple for the
625	        # position and each pickup/dropoff, and a mutable list of tuple cells
626	        # for the route. The normalized copies are committed together only
627	        # after every robot and task passed validation, so a rejection -- even
628	        # one buried in a later robot's route or task point -- never touches
629	        # the caller's objects: a fleet whose routes fail is rejected with
630	        # every robot still holding the original position object and route and
631	        # every task still holding its original pickup/dropoff containers. See
632	        # :meth:`_normalize_initial_routes`,
633	        # :meth:`_normalize_start_positions` and
634	        # :meth:`_normalize_task_coordinates`.
635	        normalized_routes = self._normalize_initial_routes(
636	            grid, robots, normalized_positions
637	        )
638	        for robot, position, route in zip(robots, normalized_positions, normalized_routes):
639	            robot.position = position
640	            robot.route = route
641	        for task, (pickup, dropoff) in zip(tasks, normalized_task_points):
642	            task.pickup = pickup
643	            task.dropoff = dropoff
644	
645	    @staticmethod
646	    def _require_unique_ids(
647	        robots: Sequence[Robot], tasks: Sequence[Task]
648	    ) -> None:
649	        """Reject a batch that names one robot id or task id more than once.
650	
651	        Each robot id may identify at most one robot within the given robot
652	        list, and each task id at most one task within the task list; the two
653	        namespaces are independent, so a robot and a task may share one string.
654	        The judgement is on the identifiers alone -- nothing else about two
655	        records can make a clash legal: identical records handed in twice are
656	        still duplicates, as are two robots differing only in position, idle
657	        state, preset route or in-flight task, and two tasks differing in
658	        pickup/dropoff points, owner or completion state (one finished and one
659	        still waiting included). A clash therefore never keeps one record,
660	        merges the two or renames anything: the whole request is rejected with
661	        a :class:`ValueError` that says whether the clash is among the robots
662	        or the tasks and quotes the duplicated id.
663	
664	        The check is read-only and runs before any normalization commits, so
665	        every caller object -- including records preceding a duplicate placed
666	        last -- keeps exactly the position, route containers, pickup/dropoff
667	        containers, bindings, mileage and flags it arrived with. Checkpoint
668	        loading keeps its own pre-existing duplicate rejection and wording in
669	        :meth:`_load_entities`.
670	        """
671	        seen_robot_ids: dict[str, int] = {}
672	        for index, robot in enumerate(robots):
673	            earlier = seen_robot_ids.get(robot.robot_id)
674	            if earlier is not None:
675	                raise ValueError(
676	                    f"duplicate robot id {robot.robot_id!r} in robot list: "
677	                    f"entries {earlier} and {index} both name the same robot; "
678	                    "each robot id may appear at most once in a construction "
679	                    "request"
680	                )
681	            seen_robot_ids[robot.robot_id] = index
682	        seen_task_ids: dict[str, int] = {}
683	        for index, task in enumerate(tasks):
684	            earlier = seen_task_ids.get(task.task_id)
685	            if earlier is not None:
686	                raise ValueError(
687	                    f"duplicate task id {task.task_id!r} in task list: "
688	                    f"entries {earlier} and {index} both name the same task; "
689	                    "each task id may appear at most once in a construction "
690	                    "request"
691	                )
692	            seen_task_ids[task.task_id] = index
693	
694	    @staticmethod
695	    def _normalize_start_positions(
696	        grid: GridMap, robots: Sequence[Robot]
697	    ) -> list[Position]:
698	        """Validate every robot's starting position and return tuple copies.
699	
700	        The position rule is deliberately the same strict rule the route
701	        waypoints use (:func:`_as_cell`): a position must be a list or tuple
702	        (the two spellings may be mixed across one batch) holding exactly two
703	        plain integers -- booleans are rejected even though they are Python
704	        ints, and floats, strings, missing components, extra components and
705	        non-pair inputs are all refused with :class:`ValueError` naming the
706	        robot and its bad position, never rounded, coerced or padded.
707	
708	        Every accepted position is additionally checked against the map: it
709	        must lie inside the grid and outside every obstacle. Two robots may
710	        not start on the same cell either; the comparison runs on normalized
711	        tuple values, so one robot spelling a cell as ``[x, y]`` and another
712	        as ``(x, y)`` is still a collision, and the error names both robots
713	        involved. Idle robots, task-bound robots and robots carrying preset
714	        routes are all checked -- no robot is skipped to make a batch pass.
715	
716	        The check is read-only: it returns a fresh tuple per robot and commits
717	        nothing itself. The caller assigns the tuples to the robots only once
718	        the whole batch (routes and task bindings included) has passed, so a
719	        later rejection leaves the caller's positions untouched, and the tuple
720	        copy means mutating an originally passed-in list after construction
721	        can never change the created fleet.
722	        """
723	        normalized: list[Position] = []
724	        occupied: dict[Position, str] = {}
725	        for robot in robots:
726	            position = _as_cell(
727	                robot.position, f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} starting position"
728	            )
729	            if not grid.traversable(position):
730	                raise ValueError(
731	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} starting position {list(position)} "
732	                    "is outside the map or inside an obstacle"
733	                )
734	            other_id = occupied.get(position)
735	            if other_id is not None:
736	                raise ValueError(
737	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} starting position {list(position)} "
738	                    f"is already occupied by robot {other_id!r}: robots cannot "
739	                    "share an initial cell"
740	                )
741	            occupied[position] = robot.robot_id
742	            normalized.append(position)
743	        return normalized
744	
745	    @staticmethod
746	    def _normalize_task_coordinates(
747	        tasks: Sequence[Task],
748	    ) -> list[tuple[Position, Position]]:
749	        """Validate every task's pickup and dropoff and return tuple copies.
750	
751	        Task points share the strict position rule (:func:`_as_cell`): each one
752	        must be a list or tuple (the two spellings may be mixed within one
753	        task and across one batch) holding exactly two plain integers --
754	        booleans are rejected even though they are Python ints, and floats
755	        (even ``1.0``), strings, nulls, missing components, extra components
756	        and non-pair inputs are all refused with :class:`ValueError` naming the
757	        task and whether its pickup or its dropoff is at fault, never rounded,
758	        padded or coerced. This runs for every task regardless of state --
759	        waiting for assignment, en route to pickup, already carrying the goods
760	        or already completed -- so a malformed point in a finished historical
761	        record is refused at construction just like one in a pending task.
762	
763	        Coordinate validity is deliberately kept separate from reachability:
764	        whether a robot can currently reach the points is never judged here, so
765	        a well-formed task whose pickup is currently unreachable keeps waiting
766	        exactly as before, and a loaded task whose pickup cell has since been
767	        closed keeps the goods and its binding -- neither is an error.
768	
769	        The check is read-only: it returns a fresh integer tuple per point and
770	        commits nothing itself. The caller assigns the tuples to the tasks only
771	        once the whole batch (positions, ownership and routes included) has
772	        passed, so a later rejection leaves the caller's tasks holding their
773	        original pickup/dropoff containers, and the tuple copy means mutating
774	        an originally passed-in list after construction can never change the
775	        created fleet. A list and a tuple naming one cell normalize to equal
776	        tuples, so they can never make a robot miss a pickup or fail a delivery
777	        merely because of the container type.
778	        """
779	        normalized: list[tuple[Position, Position]] = []
780	        for task in tasks:
781	            pickup = _as_cell(task.pickup, f"task {task.task_id!r} pickup")
782	            dropoff = _as_cell(task.dropoff, f"task {task.task_id!r} dropoff")
783	            normalized.append((pickup, dropoff))
784	        return normalized
785	
786	    @staticmethod
787	    def _validate_task_ownership(robots: Sequence[Robot], tasks: Sequence[Task]) -> None:
788	        """Reject impossible initial bindings between robots and tasks.
789	
790	        The very same ownership requirements back direct construction and
791	        checkpoint loading, so they live in exactly one place. The mutual
792	        binding only governs work still in progress:
793	
794	        * A robot that declares a task must name a task that exists, is not
795	          completed yet, and is assigned back to that same robot.
796	        * An unfinished task that names an owner must name an existing robot
797	          whose current task it is; an unfinished task with the goods already
798	          collected additionally must have an owner.
799	        * A robot can therefore never be claimed by two unfinished tasks: the
800	          second task's owner points at a robot that executes another task.
801	        * A completed task must carry the picked-up mark *and* a historical
802	          owner (a non-null ``assigned_robot``); see below.
803	
804	        Completed tasks are history, not work in progress, but the history must
805	        still be coherent: a finished task must carry both the picked-up mark
806	        and the id of the robot that finished it -- ``None`` means "no record",
807	        never an anonymous completion, even when the pickup point and the
808	        dropoff coincide. Neither gap is repaired (the owner is not filled in,
809	        the pickup mark is not flipped, nothing is reassigned or dropped); the
810	        fleet is rejected as a whole with a :class:`ValueError` naming the task
811	        and the exact contradiction. The historical owner itself is bound by
812	        none of the in-progress rules: it need not be idle or name the task
813	        back, may already work a new task, may have finished several tasks, and
814	        may even be absent from the fleet, so historical records never occupy a
815	        robot or take part in new task assignment. Unassigned, not-yet-collected
816	        tasks simply wait -- even when no robot can reach them -- and are not an
817	        ownership error. Nothing here rewrites a binding or drops a task; an
818	        inconsistent input is rejected as a whole, leaving the caller's objects
819	        untouched.
820	        """
821	        robot_by_id = {robot.robot_id: robot for robot in robots}
822	        task_by_id = {task.task_id: task for task in tasks}
823	        for robot in robots:
824	            if robot.task_id is None:
825	                continue
826	            task = task_by_id.get(robot.task_id)
827	            if task is None:
828	                raise ValueError(
829	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} executes unknown task "
830	                    f"{robot.task_id!r}"
831	                )
832	            if task.completed:
833	                raise ValueError(
834	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} executes task {task.task_id!r} "
835	                    "that is already completed"
836	                )
837	            if task.assigned_robot != robot.robot_id:
838	                raise ValueError(
839	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} executes task {task.task_id!r} "
840	                    f"but the task is assigned to {task.assigned_robot!r}"
841	                )
842	        for task in tasks:
843	            if task.completed:
844	                # A finished task is a fixed historical record: the goods must
845	                # have been collected and a historical finishing robot must be
846	                # named. The very same requirement backs direct construction
847	                # and checkpoint recovery, so a document that could never be
848	                # loaded again can never be built in the first place. This is
849	                # judged purely from the record -- even a task whose pickup
850	                # point equals its dropoff is not presumed collected -- and the
851	                # recorded robot is history only: it is never looked up, so it
852	                # may be retired, idle or already busy with another task, and
853	                # several completed tasks may name the same robot without ever
854	                # counting as occupying it.
855	                if not task.picked_up:
856	                    if task.assigned_robot is None:
857	                        raise ValueError(
858	                            f"task {task.task_id!r} is marked completed but was "
859	                            "never picked up and has no historical assigned robot"
860	                        )
861	                    raise ValueError(
862	                        f"task {task.task_id!r} is marked completed but never "
863	                        "picked up, even though historical robot "
864	                        f"{task.assigned_robot!r} is recorded for it"
865	                    )
866	                if task.assigned_robot is None:
867	                    raise ValueError(
868	                        f"task {task.task_id!r} is marked completed and picked up "
869	                        "but has no historical assigned robot"
870	                    )
871	                continue
872	            if task.picked_up and task.assigned_robot is None:
873	                raise ValueError(
874	                    f"task {task.task_id!r} is picked up but has no assigned robot"
875	                )
876	            if task.assigned_robot is not None:
877	                owner = robot_by_id.get(task.assigned_robot)
878	                if owner is None:
879	                    raise ValueError(
880	                        f"task {task.task_id!r} is assigned to unknown robot "
881	                        f"{task.assigned_robot!r}"
882	                    )
883	                if owner.task_id != task.task_id:
884	                    raise ValueError(
885	                        f"task {task.task_id!r} claims robot {owner.robot_id!r} "
886	                        f"but the robot executes {owner.task_id!r}"
887	                    )

889	    @staticmethod
890	    def _normalize_initial_routes(
891	        grid: GridMap,
892	        robots: Sequence[Robot],
893	        positions: Sequence[Position],
894	    ) -> list[list[Position]]:
895	        """Validate every remaining route and return normalized copies.
896	
897	        Every robot is checked, idle or task-bound, via the single shared walk
898	        validator :func:`_validate_route_walk` -- the same coordinate shape,
899	        map-walkability and one-orthogonal-step rule checkpoint recovery uses
900	        -- so a walking rule never has to be changed in two places. The outer
901	        route may be a list or tuple and each waypoint may itself be a list or
902	        tuple of two plain integers -- booleans are not integers here, and
903	        wrong lengths or element types raise :class:`ValueError` instead of
904	        leaking unpacking or hashing failures. The forms may be mixed freely;
905	        only the coordinate order matters, not the container types.
906	
907	        *positions* holds the already-normalized tuple starting positions from
908	        :meth:`_normalize_start_positions`, paired one-to-one with *robots*:
909	        every route is walked from the tuple form so a first waypoint equal to
910	        the start cell is recognized regardless of how the caller spelled
911	        either container.
912	
913	        Accepted routes are returned as mutable lists of tuple cells, the one
914	        shape the rest of the engine relies on (head consumption with
915	        ``pop(0)`` and hashable cells for road and occupancy checks). Empty
916	        lists and tuples both normalize to an empty route. Routes need not be
917	        shortest paths and may revisit cells, and traffic (a route crossing
918	        another robot's cell, or routes sharing a cell) is left to execution:
919	        only walkability on the given map is judged.
920	
921	        The check is read-only -- :func:`_validate_route_walk` builds fresh
922	        lists, and the caller commits them itself only once every robot has
923	        passed, so a rejected fleet is rejected as a whole: an error on a
924	        later robot or at the end of a route never truncates, pads, reorders
925	        or otherwise modifies an earlier robot or any caller object. The
926	        shared walk check says nothing about tasks; direct construction keeps
927	        accepting any walkable route, while checkpoint loading keeps its own
928	        stricter validation that also covers the pickup/dropoff rules.
929	        """
930	        normalized: list[list[Position]] = []
931	        for robot, position in zip(robots, positions):
932	            route = robot.route
933	            if not isinstance(route, (list, tuple)):
934	                raise ValueError(
935	                    f"robot {robot.robot_id!r} remaining route must be a list "
936	                    "of [x, y] waypoints"
937	                )
938	            normalized.append(
939	                _validate_route_walk(
940	                    grid,
941	                    position,
942	                    route,
943	                    robot_id=robot.robot_id,
944	                    checkpoint=False,
945	                )
946	            )
947	        return normalized

953	    def modify_obstacles(
954	        self,
955	        added: Sequence[Position] = (),
956	        removed: Sequence[Position] = (),
957	    ) -> dict[str, object]:
958	        """Close and/or reopen cells without advancing the simulation.
959	
960	        The whole request is validated before anything changes: coordinates
961	        must be two plain integers (booleans are rejected), lie inside the
962	        map, no cell may appear in both lists, and newly added obstacles may
963	        not cover a robot's current cell. Duplicate coordinates inside one
964	        batch are processed once. Adding an existing obstacle or removing a
965	        traversable cell is a no-op. Invalid requests raise :class:`ValueError`
966	        and leave every part of the state untouched.
967	
968	        Assigned unfinished tasks keep their robot: routes are replanned
969	        against the new map, or, when a required point is unreachable, cleared
970	        while the task is suspended. No tick is recorded, no robot moves and no
971	        distance is accumulated.
972	        """
973	        add_cells = self._normalize_cells(added, "added")
974	        remove_cells = self._normalize_cells(removed, "removed")
975	        conflict = set(add_cells) & set(remove_cells)
976	        if conflict:
977	            cell = sorted(conflict)[0]
978	            raise ValueError(
979	                f"cell {list(cell)} is both added and removed in the same request"
980	            )
981	        occupied = {robot.position for robot in self.robots.values()}
982	        for cell in add_cells:
983	            if cell in occupied:
984	                raise ValueError(
985	                    f"cannot add obstacle at {list(cell)}: a robot currently occupies it"
986	                )
987	        return self._apply_map_change(add_cells, remove_cells)
988	
989	    def _normalize_cells(self, cells: Sequence[Position], label: str) -> list[Position]:
990	        if isinstance(cells, (str, bytes)) or not isinstance(cells, (list, tuple)):
991	            raise ValueError(f"{label} cells must be provided as a list of [x, y] pairs")
992	        seen: set[Position] = set()
993	        ordered: list[Position] = []
994	        for index, cell in enumerate(cells):
995	            position = _as_cell(cell, f"{label} cell {index}")
996	            if not self.grid.contains(position):
997	                raise ValueError(f"{label} cell {list(position)} lies outside the map")
998	            if position in seen:
999	                # Batch-internal duplicates are handled once, not rejected.
1000	                continue
1001	            seen.add(position)
1002	            ordered.append(position)
1003	        return ordered
1004	
1005	    def _apply_map_change(
1006	        self, added: list[Position], removed: list[Position]
1007	    ) -> dict[str, object]:
1008	        obstacles = set(self.grid.obstacles)
1009	        actual_added = [cell for cell in added if cell not in obstacles]
1010	        obstacles.update(actual_added)
1011	        actual_removed = [cell for cell in removed if cell in obstacles]
1012	        obstacles.difference_update(actual_removed)
1013	        if not actual_added and not actual_removed:
1014	            return self._map_change_record(self._map_sequence, [], [])
1015	
1016	        # Everything below only runs once the batch was fully validated and is
1017	        # known to change the map.
1018	        self.grid = GridMap(self.grid.width, self.grid.height, frozenset(obstacles))
1019	        self._map_sequence += 1
1020	        record = self._map_change_record(self._map_sequence, actual_added, actual_removed)
1021	        self.map_changes.append(copy.deepcopy(record))
1022	        self.replay.append(copy.deepcopy(record))
1023	        self._reroute_after_map_change()
1024	        self._reconcile_traffic_waits_after_map_change()
1025	        return copy.deepcopy(record)
1026	
1027	    def _map_change_record(
1028	        self, sequence: int, added: list[Position], removed: list[Position]
1029	    ) -> dict[str, object]:
1030	        return {
1031	            "type": "map_change",
1032	            "tick": self.tick,
1033	            "sequence": sequence,
1034	            "added": [list(cell) for cell in added],
1035	            "removed": [list(cell) for cell in removed],
1036	        }

1038	    def _plan_route(
1039	        self, robot: Robot, task: Task, start: Position | None = None
1040	    ) -> list[Position] | None:
1041	        """Shortest current->pickup->dropoff route, or None if unreachable.
1042	
1043	        *start* overrides the robot's current position, which is how sidestep
1044	        candidates are evaluated without moving the robot first. The
1045	        pickup/delivery rule itself is shared with first-time assignment and
1046	        checkpoint validation via :func:`_plan_task_route`.
1047	        """
1048	        origin = robot.position if start is None else start
1049	        return _plan_task_route(self.grid, origin, task)
1050	
1051	    def _reroute_after_map_change(self) -> None:
1052	        for task in self.tasks.values():
1053	            if task.completed or task.assigned_robot is None:
1054	                continue
1055	            robot = self.robots[task.assigned_robot]
1056	            if robot.task_id != task.task_id:
1057	                continue
1058	            route = self._plan_route(robot, task)
1059	            if route is None:
1060	                robot.route = []
1061	                self.paused_tasks.add(task.task_id)
1062	            else:
1063	                # Only the route is refreshed here; pickup/delivery are
1064	                # confirmed at step start (or were already recorded).
1065	                robot.route = route
1066	                self.paused_tasks.discard(task.task_id)
1067	
1068	    def _recover_paused_tasks(self) -> None:
1069	        """Resume tasks suspended by map unreachability where possible."""
1070	        for task_id in sorted(self.paused_tasks):
1071	            task = self.tasks.get(task_id)
1072	            if task is None or task.completed or task.assigned_robot is None:
1073	                self.paused_tasks.discard(task_id)
1074	                continue
1075	            robot = self.robots[task.assigned_robot]
1076	            if robot.task_id != task.task_id:
1077	                self.paused_tasks.discard(task_id)
1078	                continue
1079	            route = self._plan_route(robot, task)
1080	            if route is None:
1081	                robot.route = []
1082	                continue
1083	            robot.route = route
1084	            self.paused_tasks.discard(task_id)
1085	            self._finish_if_arrived(robot)

1091	    def _route_cells(self, exclude_id: str) -> set[Position]:
1092	        """Cells every robot except *exclude_id* still plans to drive through."""
1093	        cells: set[Position] = set()
1094	        for robot in self.robots.values():
1095	            if robot.robot_id != exclude_id:
1096	                cells.update(robot.route)
1097	        return cells

1099	    def _safe_side_cells(
1100	        self,
1101	        robot: Robot,
1102	        occupied: Mapping[Position, str],
1103	        reserved: Mapping[Position, str],
1104	        forbidden: Iterable[Position] = (),
1105	    ) -> Iterator[Position]:
1106	        """Adjacent cells *robot* may actually side-step onto this tick.
1107	
1108	        The very same safety rule backs every side-step decision -- an idle
1109	        robot yielding for someone, a busy robot dodging a blocker itself, and
1110	        the hypothetical leave checks behind a retreat -- so the shared
1111	        conditions live exactly here. A cell qualifies only when it:
1112	
1113	        * lies inside the map with no obstacle (``GridMap.neighbors`` already
1114	          skips anything else),
1115	        * is held by no robot in the given (possibly hypothetical) layout,
1116	        * was not reserved by a move that already happened this tick,
1117	        * lies on no other robot's remaining route (the moving robot's own
1118	          route is excluded), and
1119	        * is not among *forbidden*: cells that are physically free but unsafe
1120	          for the caller's scenario, such as the requester's own cell (a
1121	          side-step there would swap the two robots within one tick) or the
1122	          retreating requester's replanned path (parking there only moves the
1123	          blockage onto a cell the requester must re-enter).
1124	
1125	        Neighbours are yielded in the deterministic ``GridMap.neighbors``
1126	        order (up, left, right, down); callers keep their own selection rules.
1127	        """
1128	        blocked = set(forbidden)
1129	        blocked.update(self._route_cells(exclude_id=robot.robot_id))
1130	        for cell in self.grid.neighbors(robot.position):
1131	            if cell in blocked or cell in occupied or cell in reserved:
1132	                continue
1133	            yield cell
1134	
1135	    def _idle_sidestep_cell(
1136	        self,
1137	        blocker: Robot,
1138	        requester: Robot,
1139	        occupied: dict[Position, str],
1140	        reserved: dict[Position, str],
1141	    ) -> Position | None:
1142	        """Free side-cell a parked blocker can yield to, or None.
1143	
1144	        Only a robot with no bound task and no remaining route is parked and
1145	        asked to yield; callers must never route a taskless-but-moving robot
1146	        here. The requester's own cell is forbidden (yielding onto it would
1147	        swap the two robots within one tick); every other safety condition is
1148	        shared via :meth:`_safe_side_cells`, so the blocker never trades one
1149	        blockage for another. The first candidate in neighbour order wins.
1150	        """
1151	        return next(
1152	            self._safe_side_cells(
1153	                blocker, occupied, reserved, forbidden=(requester.position,)
1154	            ),
1155	            None,
1156	        )
1157	
1158	    def _self_sidestep(
1159	        self,
1160	        robot: Robot,
1161	        task: Task | None,
1162	        occupied: dict[Position, str],
1163	        reserved: dict[Position, str],
1164	        already_moved: frozenset[str] = frozenset(),
1165	    ) -> tuple[Position, list[Position]] | None:
1166	        """Best side cell plus replanned route for a blocked robot, or None.
1167	
1168	        Only cells off every other robot's planned route qualify, and only if
1169	        the task remains reachable from there. A candidate that merely retreats
1170	        along the corridor only to face the very same blocker again on the next
1171	        tick is rejected too: such a move records mileage and gets undone
1172	        forever instead of making progress, even when more empty cells stretch
1173	        out behind the robot. Candidates are ranked by replanned route length
1174	        with the deterministic neighbor order (up, left, right, down) breaking
1175	        ties. *already_moved* names robots that have used their one move of
1176	        this tick and therefore cannot vacate a cell to resolve the block.
1177	        """
1178	        if task is None or task.completed:
1179	            return None
1180	        destination = robot.route[0]
1181	        blocker_id = occupied.get(destination)
1182	        if blocker_id is None:
1183	            blocker_id = reserved.get(destination)
1184	        best: tuple[Position, list[Position]] | None = None
1185	        best_length = 0
1186	        # Candidates arrive in neighbour order (up, left, right, down), so the
1187	        # first candidate of the minimum replanned length automatically keeps
1188	        # that order as the tie break.
1189	        for cell in self._safe_side_cells(robot, occupied, reserved):
1190	            route = self._plan_route(robot, task, start=cell)
1191	            if route is None:
1192	                continue
1193	            if (
1194	                blocker_id is not None
1195	                and blocker_id != robot.robot_id
1196	                and self._is_bounceback_retreat(
1197	                    robot, cell, route, blocker_id, occupied, reserved, already_moved
1198	                )
1199	            ):
1200	                # The replanned route immediately returns through the cell the
1201	                # robot is vacating and the blocker cannot use that opening to
1202	                # leave: the move would be undone on the next tick.
1203	                continue
1204	            if best is None or len(route) < best_length:
1205	                best = (cell, route)
1206	                best_length = len(route)
1207	        return best
1208	
1209	    def _is_bounceback_retreat(
1210	        self,
1211	        robot: Robot,
1212	        side: Position,
1213	        replanned: Sequence[Position],
1214	        blocker_id: str,
1215	        occupied: dict[Position, str],
1216	        reserved: dict[Position, str],
1217	        already_moved: frozenset[str],
1218	    ) -> bool:
1219	        """Whether stepping to *side* only sends the robot back to the block.
1220	
1221	        A retreat is futile when the replanned route leads straight back through
1222	        the robot's current cell and still runs through the blocker's cell (so
1223	        the side move is undone next tick with the same blocker ahead) while
1224	        the blocker cannot leave its own cell through the gap that opens up.
1225	        A route that bypasses the blocker entirely is a genuine detour and is
1226	        never rejected here.
1227	        """
1228	        if not replanned or replanned[0] != robot.position:
1229	            return False
1230	        blocker = self.robots.get(blocker_id)
1231	        if blocker is None or blocker.position not in replanned:
1232	            return False
1233	        # Hypothetical end-of-tick layout: the requester has vacated its cell
1234	        # and stands on the candidate side cell.
1235	        hyp_occupied = dict(occupied)
1236	        del hyp_occupied[robot.position]
1237	        hyp_occupied[side] = robot.robot_id
1238	        # The requester only gets back onto its route by driving through these
1239	        # cells, so a blocker may only "leave" by driving on, never by parking
1240	        # on the replanned route. The requester cannot make a second move
1241	        # within this tick, and neither can a robot that already moved.
1242	        blocked_path = frozenset(replanned)
1243	        return not self._can_vacate(
1244	            blocker,
1245	            robot,
1246	            hyp_occupied,
1247	            reserved,
1248	            frozenset({robot.robot_id}) | already_moved,
1249	            blocked_path,
1250	        )
1251	
1252	    def _side_exit_cells(
1253	        self,
1254	        robot: Robot,
1255	        task: Task,
1256	        occupied: dict[Position, str],
1257	        reserved: dict[Position, str],
1258	        blocked_path: frozenset[Position],
1259	    ) -> Iterator[tuple[Position, list[Position]]]:
1260	        """Side cells a busy robot could escape to, with their replanned routes.
1261	
1262	        Only cells off every other robot's planned route that keep the robot's
1263	        task reachable are offered, in deterministic neighbour order. Whether
1264	        such a cell is a genuine way out -- or just moves the robot aside for
1265	        one tick before it is driven back onto the same blocked corridor -- is
1266	        judged by the caller as it scans the candidates.
1267	        """
1268	        for side_cell in self._safe_side_cells(
1269	            robot, occupied, reserved, forbidden=blocked_path
1270	        ):
1271	            route = self._plan_route(robot, task, start=side_cell)
1272	            if route is not None:
1273	                yield side_cell, route

1275	    def _can_vacate(
1276	        self,
1277	        blocker: Robot,
1278	        requester: Robot,
1279	        occupied: dict[Position, str],
1280	        reserved: dict[Position, str],
1281	        checking: frozenset[str],
1282	        blocked_path: frozenset[Position],
1283	    ) -> bool:
1284	        """Whether *blocker* can leave its cell this tick in the given layout.
1285	
1286	        A parked blocker (no task and no remaining route) leaves only by
1287	        yielding onto a safe side cell for the requesting robot; a moving
1288	        blocker -- task-bound, or taskless but still driving a remaining route
1289	        -- leaves by driving onto its next waypoint (possibly following a
1290	        chain of robots that all move this tick); a task-bound one may also
1291	        sidestep onto a free adjacent cell itself. Robots paused by map
1292	        unreachability never move. *checking* names robots already on the
1293	        dependency chain (including robots that used their one move of this
1294	        tick), so meeting one again closes a cyclic dependency -- a head-on
1295	        deadlock, or the requester itself -- and never proves an exit merely
1296	        because every robot on the cycle still carries a route.
1297	        *blocked_path* holds the cells the retreating requester must drive
1298	        back through: another robot parking there only moves the blockage, so
1299	        such sidesteps do not count as leaving (driving on along the cell on
1300	        the blocker's own route does).
1301	
1302	        A task-bound blocker's own side step is judged by the same standard as
1303	        the requester's retreat: it counts as leaving only when the replanned
1304	        route from the side cell does not lead straight back through the cell
1305	        being vacated into another robot that cannot get out of the way
1306	        either. A side cell the blocker must leave again on the next tick to
1307	        re-face the very same unyielding jam further down the corridor is no
1308	        way out, so it never justifies the retreat behind it.
1309	
1310	        The follow chain can run through an arbitrarily long legal queue, so
1311	        the search is an explicit stack rather than Python recursion: a queue
1312	        of twelve hundred robots ending at a parked robot with no side cell
1313	        must report "cannot vacate" from a normal ``step()`` instead of
1314	        raising :class:`RecursionError`. Each frame is
1315	        ``(robot, occupied, checking, blocked_path, resume)``: a nested
1316	        hypothetical (the blocker having stepped aside) works with its own
1317	        layout and no-go cells, so both travel with the frame. *resume* is
1318	        ``None`` on a frame's first visit and afterwards holds the robot's
1319	        not-yet-tried side-exit candidates as a stateful iterator. A frame
1320	        examined for the first time first tries the free-waypoint and
1321	        follow-chain rules; only when the chain ahead comes back empty does it
1322	        resume at its own side-cell scan, continuing exactly where that scan
1323	        stopped -- the order the single recursive call imposed.
1324	        """
1325	        frame = (blocker, occupied, checking, blocked_path, None)
1326	        stack: list[
1327	            tuple[
1328	                Robot,
1329	                dict[Position, str],
1330	                frozenset[str],
1331	                frozenset[Position],
1332	                Iterator[tuple[Position, list[Position]]] | None,
1333	            ]
1334	        ] = [frame]
1335	        while stack:
1336	            current, cur_occupied, cur_checking, cur_blocked_path, resume = stack.pop()
1337	            if current.robot_id in cur_checking:
1338	                # The chain has folded back onto a robot it already depends
1339	                # on: a cycle cannot vacate itself. The frame that followed
1340	                # this one simply resumes with its own side-cell options.
1341	                continue
1342	            task = self.tasks[current.task_id] if current.task_id is not None else None
1343	            if task is not None and task.task_id in self.paused_tasks:
1344	                continue
1345	            if not current.route:
1346	                if task is not None:
1347	                    # A busy robot with no route left only arrives/finishes this
1348	                    # tick; it never drives or sidesteps for anyone.
1349	                    continue
1350	                # A parked robot (no task and no remaining route) leaves only by
1351	                # yielding onto a safe side cell for the requesting robot; it does
1352	                # so onto the first safe cell in neighbour order. When that
1353	                # particular cell sits on the path the retreating requester must
1354	                # re-enter, parking there only relocates the blockage instead of
1355	                # clearing it, so it does not count as leaving.
1356	                side = self._idle_sidestep_cell(current, requester, cur_occupied, reserved)
1357	                if side is not None and side not in cur_blocked_path:
1358	                    return True
1359	                continue
1360	            if resume is None:
1361	                ahead = current.route[0]
1362	                if (
1363	                    self.grid.traversable(ahead)
1364	                    and ahead not in cur_occupied
1365	                    and ahead not in reserved
1366	                ):
1367	                    return True
1368	                occupant_id = cur_occupied.get(ahead) or reserved.get(ahead)
1369	                if (
